prompt: A chess program whose rules were all written by hand. Is it AI?

choices.text: Yes, it is part of the field
choices.why: Right. Much of AI does not learn at all. Learning from examples is the part called machine learning.

choices.text: No, since AI means a large language model
choices.why: A language model is one kind of system inside one part of the field.

choices.text: No, since nothing in it was learnt from data
choices.why: Learning is what makes it machine learning. AI is wider than that.

choices.text: Only if it beats a human champion at the game
choices.why: How well it plays does not decide which field it belongs to.

prompt: Where does `toylm` sit among these terms?
hint: It learnt from data. Does it have a neural network?

choices.text: Deep learning, since it predicts the next word
choices.why: Predicting the next word does not need a neural network. `toylm` does it with counts.

choices.text: Outside AI altogether, since it is only counting
choices.why: Counting what follows what in a corpus is learning from data, in its simplest form.

choices.text: A large language model, at a smaller scale
choices.why: A large language model is a deep-learning model with learnt weights. `toylm` has counts.

choices.text: Machine learning, outside deep learning
choices.why: Right. It learnt its counts from a corpus, so it is machine learning, and it has no neural network, so it is not deep learning.

prompt: Match each term to an example from this lesson.
hint: The figure has one example per box.

pairs.right: a chess program with hand-written rules
a spam filter trained on examples
the model behind a chat assistant

prompt: Why is a spam filter not called generative?

choices.text: It was trained on examples written by people
choices.why: So was every generative model. Training data does not decide it.

choices.text: It outputs a label, not new content
choices.why: Right. Generative models produce new text, images, audio or code.

choices.text: It is too small to be generative
choices.why: Size has nothing to do with it. The kind of output does.

choices.text: It runs on a mail server and not in a browser
choices.why: Where it runs does not change what it produces.

prompt: In what sense is a large language model narrow, according to this lesson?
hint: How many things does it do, underneath?

choices.text: It only works in English
choices.why: Language models work in many languages. Narrow here is about the mechanism, not the language.

choices.text: It does one thing, next-token prediction, that covers many tasks
choices.why: Right. The breadth comes from how many tasks can be written as text; the mechanism stays one.

choices.text: It can answer questions on one subject only
choices.why: It answers on a great many subjects. That breadth is what makes the one mechanism easy to forget.

choices.text: It is not narrow in any sense: it is already general
choices.why: The lesson says the opposite: one task underneath, however wide the output looks.

prompt: AGI is a ___, not a system that exists: there is no agreed definition and no agreed test for it.
hint: What kind of thing is it, if nobody has built it?

prompt: Which of these can you say about AGI on the evidence of this lesson? Choose all that apply.
hint: Separate what can be checked from what is argued.

choices.text: Different organisations define it differently
choices.why: Yes: some by ability, some by economic value, some by learning new tasks.

choices.text: A claim that a system is AGI cannot be checked without an agreed test
choices.why: Yes. Without a test it can only be argued.

choices.text: It is expected within a few years
choices.why: That is a prediction. This course makes none.

choices.text: It has a precise definition everyone accepts
choices.why: There is no agreed definition.

prompt: What does this lesson say a large language model demonstrably is?

choices.text: A database of facts with a fluent interface on top
choices.why: There is no database inside. Lesson 8: the weights are numbers, not records.

choices.text: A general intelligence that has not been switched on fully
choices.why: That is a claim about a goal, not a description of what exists.

choices.text: A next-token predictor with learnt weights
choices.why: Right. That is checkable, and it stays true however impressive the output is.

choices.text: A search engine that rewrites what it finds
choices.why: It does not search unless a tool is added, lesson 6.

prompt: `toylm` scored three out of three on `bench.txt`. Why does that score mean little?
hint: Look at what it answered on `new.txt`.

choices.text: Three questions is too few for any test
choices.why: Few questions is a weakness, and the deeper problem is what the test rewards.

choices.text: It was lucky
choices.why: It would score three out of three every time. It answers `yes` to anything after `answer :`.

choices.text: It says `yes` to everything
choices.why: Right. Every answer in the test was `yes`, so the test measured whether it says `yes`.

choices.text: The questions were in English
choices.why: The language is not the problem. The answers were all the same and in the training data.

prompt: How many times does `grep -c` find `question : is the bread fresh` in `corpus.txt`?

hint: Where did the bread question come from?

choices.text: Test questions ending up in the training data
choices.why: Right. A high score then measures memory, not ability.

choices.text: Errors in the answer key of a benchmark
choices.why: A wrong key is a different problem. Contamination is about where the questions have been.

choices.text: Training data that contains offensive text
choices.why: That is a real issue, and a different one.

choices.text: A model's answers leaking into other people's chats
choices.why: That is a privacy question, not a measurement one.

prompt: Of the ten samples `toylm` gave for when the café opens, how many said `at seven`?
A launch video shows a model solving a hard problem perfectly. What does that show, on its own?

choices.text: That it reliably solves problems of that kind
choices.why: Reliably needs many attempts and a count. A video is one.

choices.text: Nothing, since demos are faked
choices.why: Most are real runs. The point is that they were chosen.

choices.text: That it will solve your problem
choices.why: Your problem was not in the video.

choices.text: That it succeeded at least once
choices.why: Right. A demo is a selected run. How reliably it succeeds needs many runs.

prompt: A vendor reports a near-perfect score on a benchmark published four years before its model was trained. Which question matters most?
hint: How old is the test, compared with the training data?

choices.text: Was the score rounded up to look better?
choices.why: Rounding moves a number slightly. It does not change what the number measures.

choices.text: Did the model answer the questions quickly?
choices.why: Speed is a separate question from whether the score means ability.

choices.text: Were the questions in its training data?
choices.why: Right. A test public for years is likely to be in the text the model read, and then the score measures memory.

choices.text: Is the benchmark a famous and widely used one?
choices.why: Fame makes contamination more likely, and is not the question to ask.

prompt: Put the steps of checking a claim about your own use in a sensible order.
hint: From the claim to your own evidence.
items: Ask whether the test could be in the training data
Run the model many times on inputs like yours
Count how often it does what you need

prompt: Which of these sentences describes reliability?

choices.text: 46 right out of 50 messages like ours
choices.why: Right. Many attempts, inputs like yours, and a count.

choices.text: It correctly sorted a tricky message in the demo
choices.why: That is one run, chosen. It shows it can.

choices.text: It scored top marks on a famous benchmark
choices.why: A score on someone else's test, which may have been in its training data.

choices.text: The vendor says it is the most capable model yet
choices.why: A vendor's claim, until somebody else measures it.

prompt: A colleague says: "It solved the puzzle in the demo, so it reasons like a person." Which reply follows from this lesson?
hint: What is the model, demonstrably, and what is a demo?

choices.text: One chosen run shows the output, not the process
choices.why: Right. A next-token predictor produced it once; how often, and why, are separate questions.

choices.text: Agreed, since only reasoning could produce a correct answer
choices.why: `toylm` produced `at seven` correctly once in ten with no reasoning at all.

choices.text: No, since language models are never right about puzzles
choices.why: They often are. The point is what one success shows.

choices.text: Agreed, if the puzzle was on a benchmark
choices.why: A benchmark puzzle may be in the training data, which makes it weaker evidence.

prompt: Who is in the best position to tell you whether a model works for your task?

choices.text: The vendor, since they built it and know it best
choices.why: They know the model; they do not know your inputs.

choices.text: A public leaderboard of benchmark scores
choices.why: A benchmark measures someone else's questions.

choices.text: The model, if you ask it
choices.why: Its answer is generated text, like any other.

choices.text: You, by testing it on many inputs like your own and counting
choices.why: Right. A measurement on your own task beats any general claim.
